skill.name: git-workflow-and-versioning
skill.description: Guides developers and AI agents through disciplined Git branching, atomic commits, worktrees, change review, releases, semantic versioning, tags, and changelogs.
skill.summary: Plan safe Git changes, maintain reviewable history, and manage releases with clear versioning and changelog practices.
skill.author: addyosmani

security_audit.summary: All 69 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown syntax, illustrative Git commands, fixed example paths, defensive secret-name checks, or sensitive-file exclusion advice. The skill contains no runtime execution, prompt injection, credential exfiltration, or network behavior; the main residual concern is user error when following destructive Git examples.

remediation.issue: Destructive reset guidance can discard uncommitted work.
remediation.suggestion: Add an explicit warning that git reset --hard HEAD permanently discards changes and require confirmation before using it.

remediation.issue: Shell examples may be copied without reviewing their targets.
remediation.suggestion: Label command blocks as illustrative and tell users to verify branches, paths, remotes, and staged changes before execution.

remediation.issue: Automated worktree creation can become unsafe if later parameterized.
remediation.suggestion: When adding automation, validate destination paths and reject user-controlled traversal sequences before invoking Git.

content.user_title: Improve Git Workflows and Release Versioning
content.value_statement: Unstructured branches, oversized commits, and unclear releases make changes difficult to review, revert, and communicate. This skill provides practical Git workflows for disciplined changes, safe collaboration, and predictable versioned releases.
actual_capabilities: Recommends short-lived branches, feature flags, and trunk-based development practices.
Structures atomic commits, descriptive messages, staged checks, and change summaries.
Explains worktree use for parallel agent or developer work.
Provides guidance for debugging with Git history, bisect, diff, log, and blame.
Maps changes to semantic version bumps, release tags, and human-readable changelogs.
limitations: It does not run Git commands, inspect a repository, or modify files by itself.
It cannot determine whether a change is breaking without project and consumer context.
Its branch and release recommendations may require adaptation to team policies.
It does not replace code review, testing, secret scanning, or deployment controls.

use_cases.title: Plan a small feature
use_cases.description: Turn a feature request into a short-lived branch plan with logical increments, tests, and commit boundaries.

use_cases.title: Coordinate parallel agent work
use_cases.description: Organize independent worktrees, branch names, merge points, and cleanup steps for multiple contributors or AI agents.

use_cases.title: Prepare a versioned release
use_cases.description: Choose a semantic version bump, create a tag plan, and draft a changelog focused on user impact and migration needs.

prompt_templates.title: Create a simple Git plan
prompt_templates.prompt: I need to make this change: [describe change]. Propose a branch name, three logical implementation slices, and a commit message for each slice.

prompt_templates.title: Split a messy worktree
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this list of uncommitted changes: [paste file and change summary]. Group them into clean atomic commits and explain the staging order.

prompt_templates.title: Coordinate parallel work
prompt_templates.prompt: We have these parallel tasks: [list tasks]. Design a worktree layout, branch names, integration order, and conflict-reduction checks.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a release
prompt_templates.prompt: Given these changes and consumer impacts: [describe changes], recommend a semantic version bump, tag message, changelog sections, and migration notes.

output_examples.input: A small validation feature needs implementation, tests, and documentation.
output_examples.output: Branch: feature/email-validation. Commits: add validation, add tests, update documentation. Each commit remains independently reviewable.

output_examples.input: A release adds a backward-compatible capability and deprecates an old endpoint.
output: Include the replacement endpoint and the planned removal version

best_practices: Keep each commit focused on one logical change and explain why it exists.
Run tests, linting, type checks, and staged-diff reviews before committing.
Treat tags and changelogs as part of the release contract for consumers.
anti_patterns: Do not combine formatting, refactoring, and feature work in one commit.
Do not commit secrets, environment files, build output, or unrelated generated files.
Do not hide breaking behavior under a patch or minor version number.

faq.question: Does this skill execute Git commands?
faq.answer: No. It provides workflow guidance and command examples for a developer or agent to review and run.

faq.question: Should every change use a feature branch?
faq.answer: Use the team default. The skill recommends short-lived branches and supports trunk-based workflows.

faq.question: How small should commits be?
faq.answer: Each commit should represent one logical, reviewable change. The suggested target is about 100 lines when practical.

faq.question: When should a version be major?
faq.answer: Use a major version when consumers must change code or behavior because of a breaking change.

faq.question: What belongs in a changelog?
faq.answer: Record user-relevant additions, changes, fixes, deprecations, removals, security updates, and migration guidance.

faq.question: Can this replace repository-specific policy?
faq.answer: No. Adapt the recommendations to repository rules, approval requirements, release automation, and deployment controls.
